parole.testo: From Middle High German -el, from Old High German -il, direct descendant of Proto-West Germanic *-il, from Proto-Germanic *-ilaz, or from dialectal variants of -lein, which as well ultimately go back to *-ilaz or to *-ilingaz.

parole.significato: Forms abstract nouns, typically of Latin/Greek stems as the counterpart to adjectives in -isch.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -icus and Ancient Greek -ικός (-ikós).
Borrowed from Italian abate or from Spanish abate. Doublet of Abt.
From Middle High German agraz, perhaps influenced by Italian agresto. Ultimately probably derived from Latin acer (“sour”). Alternatively from Latin agrestis (“coarse”).

From Middle High German arm, from Old High German arm, from Proto-West Germanic *arm, from Proto-Germanic *armaz, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erH- (“to be sparse”) or alternatively from Proto-Indo-European *h₃erbʰ-, whence English orphan. Cognate with Old English earm.
From Latin asterismus, from aster + -ismus or from Ancient Greek ἀστερισμός (asterismós), this from ἀστήρ (astḗr) and -ισμός (-ismós).
Borrowed from Latin Atlās or from Ancient Greek Ἄτλας (Átlas), from the name of the mythological figure Ἄτλας (Átlas, “Bearer (of the Heavens)”).

15th century, semantically after Italian banco, banca (“bench” and “bank”), from Old High German bank (etymology 1 above). Late 17th century, from Dutch berebery (1612), beriberij (1631), possibly through French béribéri (1665). parole.significato: blossom, flower (reproductive structure on plants, often scented and/or colourful)
parole.testo: From Middle High German blüete, from older bluot, from Old High German bluot, from Proto-Germanic *blōdiz (“blossom, sprout”). From Low German (e.g. Westphalian, East Frisian) and Central Franconian dialects. First attested as Dutch bohay in 1573 (now in the form poeha). Possibly of common origin with French brouhaha, be this onomatopoeic or from Hebrew בָּרוּךְ הַבָּא (bārûḵ hab-bā, literally “blessed be he who comes”); se
Either from French botte or Polish bot, in both cases ultimately from Old French bote (“boot”).

From Middle High German buoche, from Old High German buohha, from Proto-West Germanic *bōku and *bōkijā (both “beech”). parole.significato: a medieval tournament game: bohort, melee
parole.testo: From Middle High German būhurt, bēhurt, or Middle Low German bohurt, burt, later the term for a ”tournament-melee”, a medieval tournament game, in which mock combat is conducted between two groups of knights, alternatively a game in which an attack was made on a pretend fortress, but also a synonym
Borrowed from Italian dignitario or French dignitaire, from Latin dignitās.
From Ancient Greek δεινός (deinós, “fearful, mighty”) and σαῦρος (saûros), in Herodot a varia lectio of σαύρα (saúra), Ionic σαύρη (saúrē, “lizard”).

parole.significato: interpreter (one who translates in real time; male or of unspecified sex)
parole.testo: From Middle High German tolmetsche (13th c.), ultimately from Proto-Turkic *tilmač (compare Turkish dilmaç). Probably borrowed through a Slavic language; compare Proto-Slavic *tъlmačь (“interpreter”), whence Russian толма́ч (tolmáč), Polish tłumacz. Alternatively through Hungarian tolmács.

parole.significato: a (small) moor in northwestern Germany (now chiefly in placenames)
parole.testo: From German Low German Dose, Döse, Dös, "moor", "light-coloured layer in a peat moor", or from its source, Middle Low German dose (“light-coloured peat”). Perhaps related to German Dost. Some sources have suggested a possible connection to dösig, but if there is any connection, it is not obvious.

parole.significato: any plant of the genus Origanum
parole.testo: From Middle High German doste, from Old High German dost, dosto (“origanum; tuft”). Further origin unknown. According to Pokorny, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tewh₂- (“to swell”), see also Norwegian tust (“tuft”), Proto-Germanic *þūmô (“thumb”). Compare Middle Low German doste (either cognat

From Middle High German elle, from Old High German elina, from Proto-West Germanic *alinu. The form elle is most readily explained as an assimilation of syncopated elne (like müller from earlier mülnære). Alternatively it can also be a backformation from apocopated eln, elen. Cognate with English el

parole.significato: to take pity on, to have mercy for
parole.testo: Most likely related to archaic German Barm (“bosom”) and has the sense of "cherishing in one's bosom," from Middle High German barm, from Old High German barm, from Proto-West Germanic *barm. Alternatively, from Middle High German erbarmen, irbarmen, from Old High German irbarmēn (“to take pity, hav
Borrowed from French évidence or Latin ēvidentia.

parole.significato: Vehmic court (medieval, chiefly Westphalian, special court for capital crimes presided by a local noble or freeman appo…
parole.testo: From northern Middle High German veme, a borrowing from Middle Low German vēme. Cognate with Dutch veem. The further origin is unknown, though a relation with either Fehde (“feud”) or Feind (“enemy”) has been considered.

parole.significato: a cloth for cleaning, especially a floorcloth
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German Feudel, Feul, Feil, either from or cognate with Dutch feil (“floorcloth”, attested 1616). Further origin uncertain. Ripuarian Fuddel (“old rag”), if related, would suggest that the d is original, whereas all of the following theories require that it is due to hypercorrection

From Middle High German ficken (“to rub, solidify, strengthen”), perhaps from Old High German *fuchōn, *fuhhōn (attested in fitafuchōn, fitafuhhōn (“to yearn for, seek or solicit fornication”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pewǵ- (“to stick, sting, stab”). The interjectional use is probably a

From Middle High German vlackern, perhaps ultimately imitative of birds' wings, or from Proto-Germanic *flakuraz (“shaking, wavering”), related to *flakurōną (“to roam, wander”), from Proto-Indo-European *plag- (“to roam, wander”), from Proto-Indo-European *pelə- (“to wander”). Or, from Proto-German
Borrowed through Low German from English flag, or from early modern Dutch vlagghe. Compare contemporary Dutch vlag. See also Old Norse flǫgra and German flackern.

parole.significato: dormer; dormer-window (roofed projection from a sloping roof with a window at the front)
parole.testo: From late Middle High German gūpe. Further origin unknown. Since the word is apparently from Rhine Franconian dialects, identity with Kuppe (“top, knoll”), itself also a Central German form, is possible. The long vowel is problematic, however, though it might be due to conflation with a related word

From Middle High German gīge, from Old High German gīga, of unclear origin. From Middle High German geræte (“consultation; equipment”), from Old High German girāti (“advice, consultation”), derived from rāt (“advice, council”). By surface analysis, ge- + Rat. From Glas (“glass”) + -ern or from Middle High German gleserīn, variant of glesīn, from Old High German glesīn, from Proto-West Germanic *glasīn.

Early 18th century. Either directly from modern French graver or through Dutch and Middle Dutch graveren (13th c.), from Old French graver, from Frankish *graban, from Proto-Germanic *grabaną. Doublet of graben.
Borrowed from German Low German grienen from Middle Low German grīnen, the Low German form of greinen “to sob, to weep”, which originally meant “to twist one′s mouth (either in joy or sadness)”.

parole.testo: From Middle High German hanthaben (1349). The earliest sense is “to keep, protect, maintain”, hence eventually a loan translation of Old French maintenir and/or Latin manūtenēre. parole.significato: small room or compartment (typically dark, stuffy and of small size)
parole.testo: Probably derived from Middle Low German kabūse (“shed”) (compare Kombüse) through conflation with another word, which may either Dutch kombof (“hovel”) or one from the root of German Koben (“stable, shed”). Commonly associated with Rotwelsch, and possibly spread by it.

parole.significato: chamber, a room for abode mediocrely furnitured
parole.testo: Depending on the region from either Upper Sorbian komorka or Polish komórka. Doublet of Kammer and Kamera.

parole.significato: to crouch, to cower, to huddle (to have positioned oneself in a compact way, with bent knees and back; sitting or squat…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Low German, eventually from Middle Low German kūren (“to lurk”, originally "to crouch, bend, sit hunched over"), whence also English cower, according to Pokorny, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“to curve, bend”), see also Proto-Germanic *kuddô (“shell, pod”). From Middle High German kerze, from Old High German kerza, charza, from either Latin cērāta (“covered with wax”) or Latin charta (“sheet of papyrus”, in this case referring to layers of birch bark from which candles were made). The latter explanation is typically preferred, though the former is sema

parole.significato: Klabautermann (a two-faced goblin believed to be both helpful and inauspicious to a ship's crew)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Low German [Term?]. Without doubt related, either originally or secondarily, to Dutch kabouter(man). Further etymology unsettled. parole.significato: to click (make a clear sound, as of a lock being closed, or two marbles striking each other)
parole.testo: 16th century, from Middle High German *klicken, attested in zerklicken (“to break an eggshell”). Either cognate with or analogous to Dutch klikken (15th c.), English click (16th c.), French cliquer (14th c.). All ultimately imitative. The computing sense is a semantic loan from English.

A Low and Central German word, from Middle Low German and northern Middle High German klinke (“latch”), from Proto-West Germanic *klinku (“latch”). 19th century, from East Central German dialects. Further origin uncertain. Plausibly from Polish kleć (“outhouse”), from Proto-Slavic *klětь. Alternatively from klitschen (“to splat, slap”), a variant of klatschen.

parole.significato: staple, cramp (U-shaped hook with pointed ends)
parole.testo: Standardized since the 17th century. From Central and Low German dialects, from northern Middle High German and Middle Low German krampe f, from Old High German crampo, Old Saxon krampo m, from Proto-West Germanic *krampō, from Proto-Germanic *krampô. Borrowed from Low German laff, which is either inherited from Middle Low German *laf (seemingly not attested) or borrowed from Middle Dutch laf (early 15th century), all probably from Proto-Germanic *laba-, from Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang loosely”). Compare modern Dutch laf (“cowardly”).

parole.significato: to spawn (to deposit numerous eggs in water)
parole.testo: From Middle High German leichen (“to jump, rise, mate, spawn”). Despite the late attestation (14th c.) plausibly inherited from Proto-West Germanic *laikan (“to jump, play”). Alternatively denominal from Middle High German leich. Equivalent to Laich + -en.

From 13th-century Middle High German lebekuoche. parole.significato: to draw lots; to draw straws; to toss up
parole.testo: From Middle High German lōzen, either derived from the noun lōz (whence German Los), or inherited from unattested Old High German *lōzōn, *hlōzōn, from Proto-West Germanic *hlutōn, from Proto-Germanic *hlutōną.

From Middle High German luoder, from Proto-Germanic *lōþr-. Perhaps related to Latin lateō (“to hide”) or from the same ultimate source as the verb laden (“to invite”), considering the sense of summoning, baiting.

parole.significato: A seabird belonging to the genera Uria of the auk family Alcidae, particularly the common guillemot, Uria aalge
parole.testo: From either Danish lom or Swedish lom, ultimately from Old Norse lómr (“loon”).

From an earlier term meaning to "lurk, lie in wait for an opportunity", from Middle High German lunger (“greedy, active, brisk, quick”), from Old High German lungar (“quick, easy”), from Proto-West Germanic *lungur, from Proto-Germanic *lunguraz (“quick, vigorous, strong”). Borrowed from French masser, probably from Arabic مَسَّ (massa, “to touch”), or from Portuguese amassar. The Arabic verb was, in French, associated with and perhaps reinforced by unrelated Ancient Greek μάσσειν (mássein, “to knead”), but direct derivation from this latter is now considered unlikely.
Either directly from Masse (“mass”) + -ieren (“-ise, -ify”) or through French masser, eventually from Latin massa.

parole.significato: to kill secretly and/or treacherously, to assassinate
parole.testo: 16th century, possibly inherited from Middle High German *miucheln, *mūcheln, from Old High German *mūhhilōn, iterative of mūhhōn (“to lurk, ambush”), from Proto-Germanic *mūkōną. The earlier existence of the iterative verb is ascertained by derivatives such as Middle High German miucheler, mūcheler

parole.significato: mule (hybrid offspring of a donkey and horse)
parole.testo: 19th century, from an Alemannic German or Austro-Bavarian dialect. Possibly from an inherited form of Middle High German mūl + the diminutive suffix -li. Alternatively from Italian mulo with its plural muli associated with that suffix. Ultimately from Latin mulus, whence also Maultier.

From Middle High German mane, from Old High German mana, from Proto-West Germanic *manu, from Proto-Germanic *manō (“mane”), from Proto-Indo-European *mon- (“neck”). parole.significato: smoke, particularly when very dense or regarded as unpleasant; fume

parole.significato: to make rough, creaky, squawky sounds

parole.significato: to squeeze, to squish (to exert strong targeted pressure on something, pushing against an obstacle or resistance)

Deverbal from rabatzen, now obsolete in favour of Rabatz machen, from Polish rąbać, alternatively or concurrently dialectal rabanzen, rabastern etc. from old ranzen, ratzen going back to Middle High German and ultimately related to onomatopoeic formations such as well-known ratschen and rasseln.
